title: How Trepanation Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain trepanation, the ancient practice of cutting or drilling a hole in the skull. They cover Paul Broca's 1870s encounter with a trepanned skull that prompted the French Anthropological Society to dispute it, the oldest known examples (about 8,000 years ago, Mesolithic), its global spread, high survival rates in prehistory versus worse outcomes in medieval and later Europe, and the surgical methods (grooving, scraping, boring and cutting). They discuss theories for why it was done (religious or magical, initiation, medical treatment of head trauma, curiosity), Hippocratic texts, the Stone of Madness painting by Bosch, the Kisi people in Kenya, the modern self-trepanation movement (Amanda Feilding, Peter Halverson, Bart Huges, the International Trepanation Advocacy Group), and a listener mail about quitting vaping.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to trepanation
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the show's age and outdated Wikipedia pages, then introduce trepanation and its link to the Time-Life Mysteries of the Unknown ads.

segments.title: Paul Broca and the trepanned skull
segments.summary: Broca received a trepanned skull in the 1870s and argued it showed an ancient surgical procedure; the French Anthropological Society disputed that non-European ancient peoples could perform it successfully. Trepanation was already a known hospital procedure in France.

segments.title: Ancient survival rates and global spread
segments.summary: Ancient trepanation had survival rates far higher than early modern rates. The oldest known example is about 8,000 years old (Mesolithic), and evidence spans Canada, North America, Ukraine, North Africa, Portugal, Scandinavia, Iraq and South America. Survival estimates and healing evidence from the Iberian Peninsula are discussed; medieval European practice had worse outcomes, possibly from unsterile reused tools. Ancient practitioners avoided the dura mater and sutures.

segments.title: Why people trepanned: theories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss proposed motives: magic and religion (including freeing demons and third-eye ideas), initiation rites, medical treatment such as epilepsy, migraines, and pressure from head trauma, and curiosity or observation after head injuries. They note John Rizzo's theory about Inca bone removal and that the motives likely overlapped, while acknowledging the difficulty of interpreting ancient minds.

segments.title: Hungarian funeral rites, the Obelion, and the cow skull
segments.summary: Neolithic Hungary may have trepanned skulls after death as a funeral rite. Trepanation at the obelion (the spot where the ponytail sits) is risky, but Russian Chalcolithic skulls show it there. A roughly 5,000-6,000-year-old cow skull from France shows the earliest known animal trepanation.

segments.title: Greek texts, Hippocratic Corpus, and the Stone of Madness
segments.summary: Written records show Greek practice; the Hippocratic Corpus describes trepanation for swelling and draining pus from skull fractures along sutures. The hosts then discuss the medieval Stone of Madness belief and Hieronymus Bosch's painting depicting its removal.

segments.title: Surgical methods: grooving, scraping, boring and cutting
segments.summary: Lopez, Carro and Pardiñas categorized methods as grooving, scraping, and boring and cutting. The hosts describe each, the scalp's pain sensitivity versus the lack of pain receptors in the skull and brain, the heat-avoidance concern when drilling, and a survival-show comparison.

segments.title: Modern self-trepanation movement
segments.summary: Amanda Feilding performed self-trepanation in 1970 and Peter Halverson followed. Bart Huges's 1962 theory linked blood volume and consciousness and claimed unfused skulls aid creativity. The International Trepanation Advocacy Group and Beckley Foundation help people get the procedure, and the British Medical Journal warned doctors. Western researchers say it has no scientific basis.

segments.title: Listener mail: Tim quits vaping
segments.summary: Listener Tim writes that an episode about child labor where Josh mentioned quitting smoking helped him quit vaping, and the hosts congratulate him.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up, advise against self-trepanation, and invite listener email.
